items.title: Do the Dems need new leadership?
items.summary:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in June 2026. | Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

Hi readers, happy Friday! Today, we’re saying farewell — for now — to “Democrats in array.” Not quite two weeks after winning the 2026 midterms by a historic margin , the party has a leadership fight on its hands. 

On Thursday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, made it official: He’s challenging current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for the title of majority leader next year, promising a bolder and more aggressive agenda for the party. 

“It is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen told MS NOW host Jen Psaki when he announced his candidacy on her show. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

Newly elected Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), each of whom defeated more leadership-aligned Democrats in their Senate primaries, are backing his bid. But Van Hollen will have an uphill climb to win the job, which is set to be decided in a closed-door vote early next month. Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, starting in 2017, and says he’s confident he will have the votes to be reelected in December.

Searching for “fighters” 

The Senate is the only chamber currently dealing with an active leadership fight, but…
items.t: Do the Dems need new leadership?

items.title: Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall
items.summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Nvidia/Japan AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo on July 16, 2026. | Philip Fong/AFP via Getty Images 

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company.

But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world. And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution.

Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies. That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution.

His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful. Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president.

This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum. It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment , who want to win an AI race against China. It includes economic populists in both parties,…
items.t: Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall

items.title: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints | Letters
items.summary:
An investigator writes that a human-written grievance at least gets to the heart of the issue immediately. Plus letters from Dexter Jandoo and Pete Bibby

Re your article (‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints.

You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complaints process is accessible to tenants, but AI-generated complaints don’t help with this. Sending a complaint can be intimidating and time-consuming, and using AI can give someone confidence, but when we speak to customers in person or over the phone, and reference the same technical language that’s in their AI-generated complaint letter, they often don’t understand what we are saying.

items.summary:
When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

items.title: Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere
items.summary:
Voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling location inside St. Patrick Parish Center in White Lake, Michigan on Election Day. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

One of the most eye-opening aspects of last week’s midterms was the new cohort of religious politicians it sent to Congress — many of them part of a wave of Democratic-leaning Christians .

Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters.

For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left. There are a few exceptions , of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way.

Key takeaways 

This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate. 

Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024. 

Jewish voters were still strongly Democratic, though there are clear signs of lower support than in previous electoral cycles. 

Other religious groups, mainline Protestants and Muslims, contributed to a diverse Democratic coalition — while evangelicals appeared less enthusiastic to turn out. 

The 2026 vote, for the first time in a while, makes that picture look less certain. Based on exit polls, county-level data, and some post-election analysis, we already have a handful of intriguing signs of change. The data is still early and…
items.t: Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere

items.title: Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis
items.summary:
If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball. Next on the list was baseball. The third-most wagered sport?

Table tennis. 

Colorado is almost certainly not an outlier. Table tennis occupies a similarly high ranking in Oregon , the only other state to provide sport-by-sport breakdowns of gambling revenue. And it’s likely true in every other state that allows sports gambling. This is a strange fact, one that’s been reported by a few local and national outlets. And beyond the bets involved, it’s also a window into where sports gambling is going, and how sports betting is morphing into something stranger and more destructive than dropping $100 on the New York Yankees to cover the spread on Saturday.

There’s the old quip that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. In some sense, this is sports betting that involves neither sports nor betting. The gambling on table tennis isn’t really on the game of table tennis. It’s on a strange simulacrum of table tennis created solely for the purpose of creating more ways to gamble on it. For many of the people involved, it’s a kind of mindless, by-the-second slot machine rather than an informed wager on a player they might think can win. Ping-pong, in other words, has been reengineered into an addictive technology.

The story of how table tennis came to occupy this outsized role in sports betting — and what it really looks like now — offers an unsettling peek at how fast all of this is moving, and how much the business…
items.t: Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis

items.title: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study
items.summary:
Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles.

In a new study, my colleagues and I used satellite tags to track young green turtles in a protected wetland in Sharjah, UAE. Our results reveal just how important these remaining natural spaces are to young turtles.

But we also found that nature can find a way to thrive in unexpected, human-made environments too. So protecting these habitats and the connections between wetlands, artificial environments and the open sea is essential to ensuring wildlife can persist in an increasingly human-shaped world.

Coastal wetlands protect our shorelines from storms, store carbon and provide important nursery habitats for marine life. Yet scientists still know surprisingly little about how marine wildlife, including turtles, sharks and rays, use these environments. Knowing where these animals feed, shelter and move helps identify which areas need protection and whether existing protected areas are working.

Our study, a collaborative effort between the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), a UAE government agency, the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre, focused on Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah, a marine protected area encompassing the last major coastal wetland ecosystem on the UAE’s east coast, which is called Khor Kalba.

Its complex wetlands support migratory wading…
items.t: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study

items.title: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong
items.summary:
Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill.

According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X, the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”.

In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems.

This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters.

items.title: Jensen Huang is out. What now?
items.summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images 

The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO. Nvidia’s board of directors announced his resignation on Thursday morning and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Huang has been making headlines all week after news broke Friday that he had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singaporean tech firm Megaspeed who the US government alleges was also a Chinese spy.

The revelation Wednesday of a second extramarital affair , this time with an Nvidia employee reporting to Huang directly, added to the pressure, and another affair came to light later on Thursday after Huang’s ouster.

The scandal has implications far beyond one company: Huang’s central role in the AI race can’t be overstated. It was his vision of an AI future that led him to pivot Nvidia from a small company making video game chips into the dominant player in making the chips that serve OpenAI , Anthropic, and Google’s computing needs.

Huang is close friends with President Donald Trump’s and a leading voice in resisting efforts to slow AI progress. And he has pushed for the US to take a less hawkish position toward China’s own AI goals , a stance now called into question by his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Among its other impacts, the news has revived efforts on Capitol Hill to further restrict chip exports to China .

To break down the national security implications of Huang’s departure, how the Trump administration is involved, and what it…
items.t: Jensen Huang is out. What now?

items.title: Is this the end of the Electoral College?
items.summary:
Boxes containing the Electoral College votes are carried into the House Chamber during a joint session of Congress to ratify the 2024 presidential election. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

I don’t know how much time you spend in the more feverish right-wing corners of the internet, but some conservative commentators are growing very alarmed about a specific Democratic policy proposal that could be nearing fruition.

It’s not abolishing ICE . It’s not nationalizing grocery stores . It’s not even investigating President Donald Trump over his reported failure to act on intelligence about his newly jobless/disgraced pal , Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang.

Instead, they’re concerned about a wonky electoral workaround called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact , which would essentially sidestep the Electoral College. (And in the words of one right-wing commentator, “effectively [rig] the system so Democrats could never lose again.”) 

NPV isn’t quite as nefarious as that (Trump won the popular vote just two years ago!), though it would revolutionize how the United States conducts presidential elections. The compact is basically an agreement between states to award their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how their own state voted. Once enough states sign on, their combined electoral votes would guarantee the presidency to whoever wins the national popular vote.

The compact has laid dormant for…
items.t: Is this the end of the Electoral College?

items.title: How the 7 healthcare workers who just got elected to Congress plan to fix our broken system
items.summary:
Newly elected members of Congress on Capitol Hill. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 

Last week’s blue tsunami carried a lot of white coats: At least seven newly elected Democrats have medical degrees or nursing careers. Pediatrician Annie Andrews of South Carolina scored one of the most shocking Senate victories of election night for Democrats, while Abdul El-Sayed (who earned a medical degree before working in public health) won the all-important Michigan Senate race. In the House, Democrats will soon welcome pediatrician Richard Pan of California , emergency room physician Amish Shah of Arizona , surgeon Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, emergency nurse Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, and oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker of Ohio.

Like many Democrats, these candidates campaigned on lowering costs, expanding health coverage, and confronting the drugmakers and healthcare corporations that they accuse of putting profits ahead of patients. They have endorsed big ideas to make healthcare better, from a public insurance option to Medicare-for-all, alongside targeted changes to drug prices and health insurance denials.

With President Donald Trump still in the White House, Democrats’ healthcare agenda faces obvious obstacles in the short term. But I spoke with Pan and Shah this week to learn how they hope to influence the healthcare conversation in Washington going forward. 

They may be politicians, but they have seen America’s broken healthcare up close. They’re hoping to help some of their new colleagues, who may not have those same experiences and may be prone to…

items.title: How science informs author Emily St. John Mandel’s fiction
items.summary:
Emily St. John Mandel in September 2016. | Ulf Andersen/Getty Images 

The world is full of unanswered questions and strange ideas. Do parallel universes exist? What would it look like if a pandemic wiped out life as we know it? Is time travel possible? 

I host the science podcast Unexplainable , where we often speak to scientists about their attempts to puzzle through life’s greatest mysteries, but academic researchers aren’t the only people wrestling with these concepts.

On the latest episode of the show, I spoke with Emily St. John Mandel, the award-winning author of Station Eleven , about her new book, Exit Party , which grapples with the question of the multiverse. We talked about how she approaches science in her fiction, and how, even if we never get clear answers to some of these strange ideas, they can still help us think deeply about ourselves and our world. 

Below is an excerpt from our conversation, edited for clarity and length. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts and Spotify , or watch us on Netflix .

Emily, you are often writing about really interesting scientific ideas. Why do you put these scientific concepts at the heart of the books that you write? 

Because they’re so interesting. I don’t have an educational background in science. I didn’t study it in school. I did work in a cancer research lab for years, so I’ve definitely hung out with scientists. I was great with grant budgets. But I could not actually tell you the mechanisms by which microRNA 335 impacts…
items.t: How science informs author Emily St. John Mandel’s fiction

items.title: The disturbing reality behind America’s milk and cheese — and the fight to end it
items.summary:
This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare. 

Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country. But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system. And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it. 

At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies . Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation. Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them. Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef. 

But whatever their ultimate market destination, the overwhelming majority of baby cows born in the dairy industry, in California and nationwide, spend their first few months of life housed alone, in individual crates or enclosures. Many of them look like this: 

Earlier this year, I wrote at length about that practice. These wooden crates provide each calf about 13 square feet of living space, less than one-tenth the size of a typical parking spot.…

On the Today programme this morning, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, a prominent leftwinger, indicated she might vote against legislation to implement the Alan Milburn proposals. She said she was concerned by the idea that the cuts would apply to people already getting sickness and disability benefits, and she said it appeared to be a breach of a promise given last year that people already getting Pip (the personal independence payment) would not lose it.

She said:

I just don’t think that you get a disabled young person into work by taking away the money that helps them to get into work.

The cuts seem to land on young disabled people, and many of them are in college already or already in work. So I don’t see how you fix the first by punishing the second.

Milburn said he concluded fundamental change was needed. He said:

The whole system needs to be changed, because the system is geared to keeping people inactive when, for young people in particular, it’s all about how can you make them active, get them earning, learning, so that they can rely on a wage rather than on a benefit. So, this is not about cutting one benefit, it’s about rebuilding the system from scratch.

He said that he decided existing claimants should be covered by the changes, not just new changes.

It’s a big rewriting of the welfare system. And obviously one of the conundrums was, ‘Should this apply to only new claimants?’

I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not…

items.title: Charity shops give far more than they take | Letters
items.summary:
Rachel Walker recalls her parents’ efforts, Phil Coughlin says donating lifted his spirits at a sad time, and Tom Stubbs champions the refugees who volunteer

Antony David Davies is absolutely right that charity shops have value in the community (Letters, 5 November). My parents coordinated an ecumenical charity shop in Huyton, Liverpool, for over 40 years. After all bills were paid, it gave away £400,000: 75% to Christian Aid for its water project in Mali and 25% to local charities nominated by the volunteers who worked there. This was in an area disadvantaged in many ways, which could easily have said it had enough problems of its own.

Instead, the shop brought Huyton’s churches together and raised awareness of suffering thousands of miles away. It gave purpose, friendship, laughter and a decent cup of Fairtrade coffee to those who worked there and those who shopped there. Tony Wilson, of Manchester Haçienda fame, was the keynote speaker at its fifth anniversary celebration, and until it closed, it offered community service placements to students working towards the Duke of Edinburgh award. Shops like this give far more than they take. The landlord, needless to say, did very well out of it.
Rachel Walker
Bath

items.title: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef
items.summary:
As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species.

This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home.

The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken.

As the years went by, commercial jetliners superseded transatlantic sea travel, and the vessel was retired and neglected for decades. Rather than facing the ignominy of a breaker’s yard, the legendary ship was bought by Okaloosa County, Florida, to turn it into a diving attraction.

The SS United States is a particularly enormous structure to introduce to the seabed – longer even than the Titanic. It will rest in around 55 metres of water,…
items.t: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef

In this and other cases, there will always be people who focus not on the claims, but on the young person and what they should have done differently. Linguistic research on how grooming actually works suggests that this instinct is exactly the result that grooming is designed to produce.

items.title: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis
items.summary:
What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit?

Across Europe, parts of the nationalist right are increasingly blurring the distinction between culture and ethnicity. The result is a view of national identity where belonging depends on where a person’s ancestors come from.

This way of thinking is called ethnonationalism – where membership of a nation depends on ethnic background or ancestry, rather than simply on citizenship or cultural identity.

In Denmark, where I live, this idea has recently taken a striking turn. A few months ago, I appeared in a televised debate opposite a former political adviser to a Danish right-wing party who, in essence and quite seriously, argued that to be Danish, you have to be able to tolerate milk.

The argument draws on the fact that the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, is more common among people with Northern European ancestry. The suggestion was that this biological trait…
items.t: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis

items.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
items.summary:
Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others?

How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation.

The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly than the other varieties. This theory, I should point out, is based on my lived experience rather than any clinical expertise or any kind of research. Sorry – I felt too ill to bother with anything of the kind.

Continue reading...
items.t: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles

items.title: How the fog of war puts journalism in the frame
items.summary:
Since the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, and during Israel’s now three-year-long retaliation against Gaza, journalism’s traditional commitment to objectivity has been on trial.

Reporting on the Israel–Gaza war has been characterised, on social media as much as in the conservative media, as biased one way or the other.

Headlines have been parsed and corrected by social media warriors while a war of words between new journalism players and traditional media has been loud and often angry. This clash has emphasised the tension between the objective reporting claimed to be practiced by legacy media and advocacy-oriented reporting that internet journalists believe delivers more truth.

In contrast, the Russian military attack on Ukraine has been reported with milder popular criticism. The privileging of one side’s narrative over the other in this conflict appears not to have attracted the same claims of media bias.

Numerous studies have shown trust declines when audiences perceive journalism to be advocating for one position over another. In addition, they have a marked preference for news that incorporates a range of views.

This led the Centre for Media Transition to examine the way Australian media have framed both international…
items.t: How the fog of war puts journalism in the frame

Compared to the other countries we looked at, the governance of England’s social care system is confused and complex. Overlapping and unclear roles leave dangerous uncertainty around who is responsible for important decisions, contributing to the inertia around reform England has struggled with for decades. The serious consequences of this were laid bare during the Covid pandemic.

The system for governing adult social care in England has evolved haphazardly and with little clear planning. items.title: Cabo Verde’s presidential election: the stakes in one of Africa’s most stable democracies
items.summary:
Cabo Verde’s presidential election takes place against the backdrop of a democratic record that remains unusual in its regional context. The country, made up of an archipelago of islands off the coast of west Africa, has sustained multiparty competition for more than three decades. It has had peaceful transfers of power and no coups or military takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Cabo Verde (population 530,000) is a semi-presidential republic in which the president is directly elected. The prime minister is appointed by the president in light of parliamentary election results, and heads a government that is politically accountable to the national assembly.

The president represents the state and safeguards the constitution, while the prime minister and the government conduct public policy.

The presidency nevertheless carries substantial political weight. The president can veto legislation, request constitutional review and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. The office also entails responsibilities in foreign affairs and national defence.

items.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope | Martin Lewis
items.summary:
There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions

Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely.

The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said: “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on.

Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the donor pool and save lives.

A mandatory “AI-edited” label on property photos on estate agency sites.

A “no wrong door” rule for councils and public bodies: report a problem anywhere, and they must pass it to the right place, rather than bouncing you from department to department, or from council to…
